reader.title: Standing Rock treaty council attack on White Cloud
bases: At a Sioux treaty council a crowd of men led by Sitting Bull rushed at a young speaker, White Cloud, who had declared he would sign, and were stopped by Chief Gall before anyone was reported hurt (A2, A1, A11).

No one was killed or reported injured: Gall halted the rush and the council broke up (A2, A3). The crowd acted without lawful authority and in large numbers, but its stated motive was White Cloud's speech in favor of the treaty, not any pretext of justice, race or tradition (A2, A12).
Every report traces to one wire dispatch from Standing Rock, printed long (A2, A4, A6), abridged (A1, A3, A8) or summarized in Dakota news briefs (A11, A12); no independent account was found.

summary.text: The Standing Rock treaty council attack on White Cloud was a rush by a crowd of Sioux, led by Sitting Bull, at a young Sioux named White Cloud during a council on the Standing Rock reservation in Dakota Territory on Saturday, September 22, 1888.
White Cloud had just told the council that he would sign a treaty that Sitting Bull and Black Thunder opposed.
Chief Gall halted the crowd before anyone was hurt, and the wire story ran widely, once under the headline "Nearly lynched at a pow-wow."
Sioux from across the reservation came by wagon and pony to a hollow a few miles below Standing Rock to consider signing a treaty brought by government commissioners.
According to the dispatch, Sitting Bull had spent several days sending runners to urge chiefs and braves to attend and oppose the treaty.
With Chief John Grass away, having been sent to Washington, Sitting Bull took the lead, a role the report said he resented Grass for holding.

Sitting Bull opened with a speech urging the Indians not to sign and hinting at treachery by the absent chief, and Black Thunder followed, saying the paper would take their land and "no sensible Indian will sign it."
White Cloud then climbed the knoll used as a speaker's stand, said the older leaders spoke "too hastily and rashly," and declared that he would sign.
After a silence, Sitting Bull made a sign to his followers, and the crowd "dashed en masse" toward White Cloud.
The dispatch said his "fate was surely sealed" had Gall not appeared at that moment and demanded order, and the Evening Star wrote that the crowd "would no doubt have killed him."
Sitting Bull and White Cloud slipped away, and Gall rebuked Black Thunder, telling him the council was for all to express their opinions.
The Indians hitched up their ponies and went home, and the dispatch predicted that Gall's breaking up of the meeting might end further councils.
No injury, arrest or official action is reported in the coverage.

The story reached the white press as a single wire dispatch from Standing Rock, printed on September 24 by the Indianapolis Journal, the Evening Star, the Evening Journal and the Waterbury Evening Democrat.
Over the following days the Omaha Bee, the Yankton Press and Dakotaian, the Monmouth Inquirer, the Perrysburg Journal, the McCook Tribune and the Mitchell Capital ran it in full or abridged form.
Dakota papers then reduced it to one-line items in weekly news roundups, the Dickinson Press calling it "an attempt to kill White Cloud."
Most versions told the episode as a dramatic council scene that favored White Cloud and Gall, one headline saying White Cloud "Nearly Loses His Life for Indulging in Free Speech."
The same coverage described the treaty's opponents in hostile terms, from the "crafty old savage" Sitting Bull to the Mitchell Capital's headline "Vicious Redskins."
Only the Evening Star used the word "lynched," in its headline.
The Evening Star's version names the absent chief "John Gall" and then has Gall appear, while the other versions name John Grass as the absent chief and Gall as the one who intervened.

The Mitchell Capital placed the council "yesterday" under a September 24 dateline, but the Indianapolis Journal's September 23 dateline and the Evening Journal's "Saturday" both point to September 22.

accounts.label: Wire report from Standing Rock
accounts.gist: After White Cloud said he would sign, Sitting Bull signalled and the whole crowd dashed toward him; his 'fate was surely sealed' had Gall not appeared and demanded order, after which the leaders slipped away and the council broke up.

accounts.label: Dakota news briefs
accounts.gist: Sitting Bull, enraged or jealous, made an attempt to kill or an attack on White Cloud, and Gall prevented it.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the dispatch as a colorful council story, 'Big Powwow of Indians... Young Chief White Cloud Nearly Loses His Life for Indulging in Free Speech', sympathetic to White Cloud and Gall.
Headlines and text cast the Sioux opposition in hostile terms: 'Vicious Redskins', 'crafty old savage', 'maddened Indians', and the Evening Star's 'Nearly lynched at a pow-wow'.

conflicts.note: Three versions agree on Saturday, Sept. 22; the Mitchell Capital's short version appears to have kept 'yesterday' under a later dateline.

versions.value: Chief John Grass was absent, having been sent to Washington; Gall then appeared
Chief John Gall was absent, sent to Washington, yet Gall 'unexpectedly appeared'

conflicts.note: The Evening Star's version is internally inconsistent and likely garbled; the other versions distinguish Grass (absent) from Gall (who intervened).

record_check.dossier: Crowd rush at a Sioux treaty council, stopped before anyone was hurt; not a lynching (mob_assault at most, and of doubtful scope)
